newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo Beobanka plans to create banking giant.
newsitem.headline: Yugo Beobanka plans to create banking giant.

text.p: Yugoslavia's largest commercial bank Beobanka said on Thursday it was ready to set up a new banking giant with other local banks and become a negotiatior in debt talks with the country's foreign creditors.
Creating a new powerful bank would help government plans to restructure the ailing banking sector which has been hit by widespread insolvency, Beobanka spokesman Zoran Pavlovic told Reuters.
"The bank is considering two scenarios, both aimed at creating a big, powerful bank, free from bad debts and ready to finance healthy parts of the economy," Pavlovic said.
"Such a bank would also become a key negotiating partner in Yugoslavia's debt talks with the International Monetary Fund (IMF), commercial bank creditors and others," he added.
Pavlovic said both scenarios had the same aim and were tailored to the requirements of the IMF. Yugoslavia is still banned from international financial institutions.
Under the first scenario, Beobanka would acquire two or three troubled banks which lost licences earlier this year.
"But there will be no acquisition until the government clearly says how it plans to tackle the issue of old hard currency savings, bad debts and surplus labour," Pavlovic said.
If those issues are settled, particularly the problem of some $4.5 billion in hard currency savings frozen in the early 1990s, Beobanka could proceed with this plan.
"In that case, we can acquire Slavija Banka and JIK Banka, even Trgovacka banka," Pavlovic said.

Unlike Slavija and JIK Banka which had their licences revoked earlier this year, Trgovacka still has its licence. But all three have enough healthy clients who would become shareholders of the newly-formed bank, he said.

The other scenario assumes a merger with an equally powerful local bank in terms of assets. The two would create a joint stock bank, with clear credit potential and the ability to operate without any legacy of the past, Pavlovic said.
"Beobanka wants to promote the bank rehabilitation scheme and take an active part in the programme."

Establishing a sound bank is seen as a way to create an institution providing funds to healthy parts of the economy. Support would be given to construction, textiles, food processing industries and agriculture.
All efforts are in line with central bank and government plans to begin a wider-scale bank rehabilitation in 1997.

Around 100 Yugoslav banks, with assets totalling 72.5 billion dinars ($13.15 billion), share the serious liquidity problems of the entire economy, shattered by almost four years of a war-related international trade embargo.
Collecting debt is the major headache for Yugoslav banks, operating in an economy with more than 23,000 insolvent companies at the end of December.
The size of their matured but unpaid liabilities stood at 5.49 billion dinars, practically matching the volume of M1 money supply of 5.5 billion dinars.

The situation was aggravated earlier this year when the central bank, enforcing measures to restore financial discipline, said it revoked licences from two large commercial banks -- Slavija Banka and JIK Banka.
Banks lose their licences if their accounts are in the red for three consecutive days or seven days in one month.
According to some unofficial estimates, at least $3 billion would be needed for a bank rehabilitation scheme in Yugoslavia.
"There is no such money in this economy, and attempts to reorganise are much cheaper," Pavlovic said. -- Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
